summary: This issue of South Korean Interim Government Activities (No. 32, prepared by the National Economic Board) covers May 1948, a month dominated by the 10 May general election, the first in Korean history, with about 91 percent of registrants voting despite communist terror. Nearly half of the 198 elected Assemblymen were rightists, Rhee Syngman became Assembly chairman, and the Assembly convened on 31 May. North Korea's 14 May electricity cutoff discredited Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic after the Pyongyang conference and cut industrial output about 75 percent, while drought threatened summer grain. The report also covers the Cheju rebellion, border incidents, sabotage, Mukden repatriates, vested property Koreanization, court reorganization, education ordinances and women's participation. Detailed tables on prices, coal, trade, petroleum, transport, power, finance and insurance give historians a month-by-month statistical baseline for the last weeks of the Interim Government.
highlights: The 10 May 1948 election, the first in Korean history, drew more than 91 percent of registrants despite communist terror; of 198 Assemblymen, nearly half were rightists and none communist.
The National Assembly convened on 31 May with all 198 members present, and Rhee Syngman won the speakership with 188 votes; Hodge and Dean spoke at the opening.
North Korea cut electricity to the South on 14 May; power distribution fell to 56.1 million KWH from 74.5 million, and overall industrial production dropped about 75 percent by month end.
The power cutoff discredited Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic, who had reported after the 19-25 April Pyongyang conference that the North promised no separate government and continued electricity.
Election violence killed four candidates, 15 election officials and 32 policemen; elections in two Cheju districts were voided as fighting on the island intensified, with 3,126 held.
Ordinance No. 192 separated the courts from the Department of Justice from 1 June, and three education ordinances were drafted for school districts and Boards of Education.
The first Mukden repatriates reached Inchon on 11 May, about 3,800 people in four ships; refugees from the north fell about 20 per cent from April.

Thirty-one border incidents with the North Korean Constabulary occurred, and communist saboteurs burned the Inchon telephone exchange and the Yongdungpo repeater station, killing two employees and a policeman.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of No. 32 (May 1948), prepared by the National Economic Board; Board members at 31 May 1948 (Chairman Wilhelm Anderson, Executive Secretary Otis T. Weaver) and a six-part table of contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: May 1948 review: the 10 May election drew 91 per cent of registrants despite communist terror, and the Assembly sat 31 May. North Korea's 14 May power cutoff cut production about 75 per cent; drought, Cheju rebellion and a 469,000,000 won note issue also noted.

sections.title: Part I. Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population and foreign affairs (about 20,041,000 people, first Mukden repatriates at Inchon) and vested property, where the Office of Property Custody prepared Koreanization and recorded 2,334 financial statements.

sections.title: Section 1. Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: South Korea's population reached about 20,041,000 by January 1948, with net migration of roughly 1,534,000. The first Mukden repatriates reached Inchon on 11 May (3,831 by month end); a new immigration ordinance was expected about 1 August.

sections.title: Section 2. Vested Property
sections.summary: The Office of Property Custody prepared Koreanization by decentralizing and training auditors. A record 2,334 financial statements arrived, the Korean Residence Management Corporation was taken over on 6 May, and sales totaled 111,225 thousand won.

sections.title: Part II. Production and Supply
sections.summary: Production and supply: summer grain forecast of 673,982 tons, May wholesale price rises, a 75 per cent production fall after the 14 May power cutoff, anthracite output of 68,612 tons in April, trade licenses and Seoul and Pusan labor disputes.

sections.title: Section 1. Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Summer grain forecast of 673,982 metric tons on 1,956,227 acres (104.1 per cent of 1947) was threatened by drought; 94,153 acres of rice land depended on power pumps. Fisheries exports to Japan were worth $4,936,162.

sections.title: Section 2. Prices
sections.summary: Seoul wholesale rice rose nearly 10 per cent to about the January level, with barley, red beans, metals and raw silk also higher. Sugar, salt and dried fish fell. Nine-city rice averaged 734 won by 25 May.

sections.title: Section 3. Industrial Production
sections.summary: The 14 May North Korean power cutoff cut overall production about 75 per cent by month end, after a strong April (2,261,906 pairs of rubber shoes from 154 plants). Paper, cement and cotton goods fell; salt rose to 28,056 tons.

sections.title: Section 4. Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output reached 68,612 metric tons in April, up 9.3 per cent, before the May power cutoff flooded the Ongjin and Haeju mines and Yong Wol fell to 6,639 tons. Bituminous imports from Japan dropped to 61,068 tons.

sections.title: Section 5. Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: The Consumer Goods Allocation Board dealt with delayed cotton cloth deliveries. May petroleum allocations included 6,936,921 liters of gasoline for elections, and salt distribution reached 27,434 tons.

sections.title: Section 6. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: May licenses (95 import, 83 export) pointed to exports near 548 million won against imports near 323 million. April private trade: imports 746 million won, exports 391 million, 99 percent of exports to Hong Kong.

sections.title: Section 7. Labor
sections.summary: At Seoul Electric, a communist-inspired strike was denied and a 29 May conference followed Maj.-Gen. Dean's fact-finding report. At Pusan, 450 stevedores stopped work on 11-12 May and a joint hiring hall replaced the honcho system.

sections.title: Part III. Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, utilities and public works: election sabotage on rail and telephone lines, a power fall from 74.5 to 56.1 million KWH after the 14 May shut-off, and a stocktaking of Public Works achievements.

sections.title: Section 1. Transportation
sections.summary: Communist sabotage around the 10 May election wrecked train No. 36 and damaged locomotives. April Transportation revenue fell 28 percent to 374.6 million won; coal received top marine shipping priority at 42.9 percent.

sections.title: Section 2. Communications
sections.summary: Saboteurs burned the Inchon telephone exchange (about 7 million won) and arsonists destroyed the Yongdungpo repeater station on 23 May, killing two employees and a policeman. April revenue fell 30.6 percent; rates rose at month end.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Utilities
sections.summary: May power distribution fell to 56.1 million KWH from 74.5 million in April; the North delivered 15.1 million before the 14 May shut-off. Daylight Saving Time began 31 May and US monitoring of dispatch 26 May.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Works
sections.summary: Public Works was credited with rebuilding the Seoul-Pusan Highway (37 bridges, 497 km, about 236.8 million won), 162 km of levees and 515 pieces of heavy equipment. May brought 153 million won in flood subsidies and 181 fires.

sections.title: Part IV. Finance
sections.summary: Government finance (note issue, overdraft, budgets and April revenue) and non-government finance (banks, loans, deposits and insurance), with the note issue up 469 million won in May.

sections.title: Section 1. Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue peaked at 33,389 million won in December 1947, rising 469 million in May. The overdraft stood at 20,232 million won. April revenue was 1,930 million against expenditure of 2,010 million.

sections.title: Section 2. Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: April data: cash balances fell 1,080 million won to 2,428.7 million; deposits reached a record 56,421 million. Loans outstanding fell 2,096 million to 30,025 million. May loans approved totaled 1,839 million.

sections.title: Part V. Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, politics, legal affairs, police and interzone matters: the 10 May election, Assembly opening on 31 May, Ordinance No. 192 on courts, election violence and 31 border incidents.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: Chief Adviser Dr. Edgar Johnson returned on 25 May from Washington after 72 conferences. The National Economic Board met four times; pay rises of 25 to 130 percent were approved from 1 June. Military Government personnel numbered 3,003.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Developments
sections.summary: The 10 May election (91% turnout, 198 seats), the National Assembly's opening, the Pyongyang conference outcome, the 14 May power shut-off's effect on Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic, and protests over Koreans in Japan.

sections.title: General Election
sections.summary: Over 91 percent of registrants voted on 10 May in Korea's first general election. Of 198 members, nearly half were rightists and none communist; two Cheju districts were voided. The average age was 47.

sections.title: National Assembly
sections.summary: On 27 May 149 members elected Rhee Syngman temporary chairman. On 31 May all 198 attended; Rhee won the speakership with 188 votes, with Shin Ik-hi and Kim Tong-won as vice-speakers.

sections.title: North-South Conference
sections.summary: Kimm Kiu-sic and Kim Koo returned from Pyongyang on 5 May after the 19-25 April conference, reporting a four-Kim agreement to oppose a separate southern government and demand withdrawal of US and Soviet forces.

sections.title: Power Shut-off
sections.summary: North Korea cut electricity to the South on 14 May, citing unpaid bills and USAFIK's refusal to send a delegation. Rightists blamed the Soviets, communists blamed the United States, and Kim Koo disclaimed knowledge of the contract.

sections.title: Koreans in Japan
sections.summary: Several South Korean parties protested treatment of Koreans in Japan as revived Japanese imperialism. Reports that Korean schools in Japan had been closed were read as an infringement of Korean rights.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Ordinance No. 192 separated the courts from the Department of Justice from 1 June, alongside Ordinances 193-197. Prison population was 22,141; Cheju trials were expedited; 49 vested-property claims were screened.

sections.title: Section 4. National Police
sections.summary: Election violence killed four candidates, 15 election officials and 32 policemen, with about 275 civilian deaths; only 68 of 13,407 booths were attacked. On Cheju-do, 3,126 were held and two districts could not vote.

sections.title: Section 5. Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Thirty-one border incidents with the North Korean Constabulary occurred, mostly near the Oe-dong dam; an American civilian was wounded on 26 May. A Soviet Yak-9 landed near Yosu; mail fell to 43,000 pieces.

sections.title: Part VI. Social
sections.summary: Health, education, culture, press opinion, youth and women: Mukden repatriation, three education ordinances, 803 election campaign performances, 33 Korean National Youth Assemblymen and 3,000,000 women voters.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Repatriation of Mukden refugees began, with four ships carrying about 3,800 people through Inchon quarantine camps. Smallpox appeared on Cheju, and Kyongsang-namdo completed 2,106 low-cost housing units.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: Three ordinances were drafted creating school districts, Boards of Education and a household-income-tax basis for school finance. The FY 1948/49 budget was 1.5 billion won; 13.9 million textbooks were printed.

sections.title: Section 3. Culture
sections.summary: Thirty election campaign teams gave 803 performances to 1,334,464 people from 7 April. The Seoul U.S. Information Center opened 29 April, and election stamps were issued 10 May.

sections.title: Section 4. Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The press debated the Pyongyang Conference and the broken power promise, then the election. Police counted 202 dead and 643 wounded from 31 March to 17 May; the Country Guard Corps was ordered disbanded on 22 May.

sections.title: Section 5. Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Thirty-three Korean National Youth members were elected to the National Assembly, against Dai Dong's 13. Audited membership reached 859,208; the FY 1948/49 allocation was 20,600,000 won.

sections.title: Section 6. Women's Activities
sections.summary: About 3,000,000 women voted on 10 May, of 3,903,293 registered women; 19 of 594 candidates were women and none was elected. The Women's Bureau ran a Mothers' School.

sections.title: Back matter
sections.summary: Blank pages, a library date-due slip stamped June 2010, and a closing source note giving the UCSF Industry Documents Library URL; no report content.
